documents.title: AI in Academics
documents.summary: The Faculty Resource Center page gives instructors sample syllabus statements for permitting, limiting or (not recommended) prohibiting AI, and a five-level AI-Integrated Assessment Scale with strategies and Canvas indicators. It sets no campus rule and leaves each instructor to choose.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule of its own; it offers sample statements ("Adjust this statement to reflect your particular parameters") and a five-level scale ("1 - No AI" to "5 - AI Exploration") for instructors to pick from, so it delegates with tiers.

units.why: The page notes ChatGPT "can write papers and essays, even art, poems, and computer code" and that detection is hard; this states a limit on control, so P82 (cannot verify) rather than P39 (detector reliability).
units.anchor: It can be challenging to detect the use of this when students submit their work

units.policy: Faculty are invited to prepare themselves and their students for the ChatGPT EDU rollout.
units.fit_note: The text announces a rollout rather than stating a use rule.

documents.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) at UCCS
documents.summary: The UCCS AI page is student-facing advice. It hopes students use AI to support learning rather than as a shortcut, asks for transparency and documentation, and covers verification, bias, energy and copyright. It defers to each faculty member's syllabus.
documents.stance_why: The page says "faculty set their own course-level AI policies" and tells students to "follow the policy outlined in the course syllabus"; it sets no campus-wide permission or ban, so it delegates.

units.why: "we hope you use it to support and enhance your education—not as a shortcut" discourages shortcut use without forbidding it: P03.
units.anchor: we hope you use it to support and enhance your education
units.frag_start: When you use AI at UCCS, we hope

units.why: Relying on AI "to produce essays, presentations, lab reports" means "you aren’t building new skills": outsourced practice undermines learning, P41.
units.anchor: means you aren’t building new skills, practicing new ways of thinking
units.frag_start: While AI can be a valuable partner

units.why: "will be less prepared for your future career" gives career readiness as a reason against shortcut use: P94.
units.anchor: you won’t learn as much and will be less prepared for your future career
units.frag_start: When Gen AI is used as a shortcut

units.why: "Always be transparent about how you’ve used AI and document your use appropriately" is a disclosure duty: P24.
units.anchor: Always be transparent about how you’ve used AI and document your use appropriately.
units.frag_start: Always be transparent about how

units.why: An "AI Use" statement "that details what AI tools you used and how you used them" names tool and manner of use, so P25 rather than plain P24.
units.anchor: details what AI tools you used and how you used them
units.frag_start: An “AI Use” statement at the end
units.policy: An 'AI Use' statement at the end of a project detailing what AI tools were used and how is good practice.

units.why: "ask your teacher if you have questions about how to document AI use" tells students to ask when unsure: P10.
units.anchor: ask your teacher if you have questions about how to document AI use
units.frag_start: you should also ask your teacher
units.fit_note: Asks about how to document, not whether use is allowed.

units.why: "faculty set their own course-level AI policies" states that instructors decide: P04.
units.anchor: faculty set their own course-level AI policies
units.frag_start: Because faculty set their own

units.why: "it’s important to follow the policy outlined in the course syllabus" makes students follow each course's rules: P78.
units.anchor: it’s important to follow the policy outlined in the course syllabus
units.frag_start: it’s important to follow the policy outlined

units.why: "others may consider any use to be academic dishonesty" warns that some courses treat any AI use as misconduct: P36.
units.anchor: others may consider any use to be academic dishonesty
units.frag_start: Some faculty may encourage AI use
units.fit_note: States that policies range from encouraging to treating any use as dishonesty.

units.why: "Asking good, specific questions and iterating with the tool" is practical prompt advice: P93.
units.anchor: Asking good, specific questions and iterating with the tool as you work
units.frag_start: Asking good, specific questions and iterating

units.why: "choose a tool that’s designed for that kind of work" advises matching the tool to the task; no type covers tool selection by task.
units.anchor: choose a tool that’s designed for that kind of work
units.frag_start: It’s important to understand what you need
units.uncovered_note: Students should choose an AI tool suited to the type of task.

units.why: "many AI tools require paid subscriptions" with advice to research tools before using them for a class is a cost-awareness note, P51 in part.
units.anchor: Research tools before deciding to use them for a class or assignment.
units.frag_start: Keep in mind that many AI tools
units.fit_note: Advises students to research cost before use; does not forbid requiring paid tools.

units.why: "You have free access to some AI tools as a UCCS student" tells students about free and discounted access: P51.
units.anchor: You have free access to some AI tools as a UCCS student.
units.frag_start: You have free access to some AI

units.frag_start: UCCS’s Kramer Family Library has more

units.policy: Every use of AI has an environmental cost, and users should be cognizant of it when weighing when and how to use AI.
